title: Now That I Have Reiterated Your Opinion, Can You Summarize Mine?
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This Admired Leadership Field Note addresses team members who are strong advocates but weak listeners, people so consumed with their own view that they argue past everyone else. The proposed remedy is a simple two-step request. The leader first summarizes the team member's view, then asks the team member to describe how the leader sees the issue. When the team member cannot do so accurately, the lesson teaches itself without scolding, and the conversation resumes only once the leader's position has been described correctly. The piece argues that listening is not a detour from persuasion but an ingredient of it, because advocates who absorb others' views make sharper and more convincing arguments. It adds that the request should be used sparingly and without judgment, as a teaching tool rather than a test, and that the strongest team members eventually adopt the practice themselves.
points: The leader models listening first by summarizing the other person's view, then invites the team member to return the favor, which turns an abstract coaching point into a concrete exercise.
When a team member fails to describe the leader's view accurately, the gap exposes itself, so the leader can correct the pattern without scolding or pointing out a flaw.
Advocacy improves after listening, because arguments that incorporate what others actually believe become sharper, more relevant and more persuasive.
The request works only when used sparingly and without judgment, as a teaching tool rather than a test, or it will feel like a trap.
The long-run goal is a team norm in which people summarize how others see an issue before they advocate, so the whole group argues better.
quotes: Leaders first summarize the team member’s view and then request they return the favor by describing the leader’s opinion on the issue. In other words, they politely ask the team member to explain how the leader sees the issue.

When the team member can’t describe the leader’s view accurately, the lesson teaches itself. The team member realizes, often with some discomfort, that they have been arguing past the leader rather than with them.
Some team members are strong advocates but weak listeners. They become so consumed with their own views that they don’t stop to pay attention to the opinions of others.
Over time, headstrong advocates learn that listening is not a detour from persuasion but a necessary ingredient of it.

When they understand how others see an issue, their arguments become sharper and more relevant. By absorbing what others actually believe and incorporating it into their advocacy, they become much more convincing.
The best leaders use this request sparingly and without judgment. In skilled hands, the request is a teaching tool, not a test.

When the idea takes hold that earning the right to be heard begins with hearing others, the whole team argues better. Team members stop talking past one another and start building on what they have understood.
